assessment.nobel_worthiness: Grossman and Helpman built the standard framework for the political economy of trade policy. The 'Protection for Sale' model gives a tractable, testable account of how lobbying shapes tariffs. It spawned a large theoretical and empirical literature and links trade theory to political economy. The same pair also did foundational work on endogenous growth and trade.
assessment.attribution: The credited pair are the clear originators and long-time co-authors of the core model and its extensions. This is clean for a two-person award. Other contributors, such as Bagwell and Staiger on trade agreements, are a distinct strand and are not needed here.
assessment.maturity: The core contributions date from the 1990s and have been tested through decades of empirical and theoretical follow-up, so the maturity is very high.
uncertainties: Helpman also appears in the firm-heterogeneity candidate (B012). The Committee may prefer to frame the award around heterogeneity or growth rather than political economy.
Empirical support for the lobbying model's precise predictions is mixed.
Trade has recently been recognised only indirectly (Krugman, 2008), so the timing is hard to judge.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: These authors built modern political economics as a formal and empirical field. Their work covers how electoral rules, constitutions and political institutions shape fiscal policy, redistribution and state capacity. It connects to development, public finance and comparative politics, and has been very influential.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central pair through their joint research programme and book, and Besley is a close third through work on state capacity, accountability and development. A three-person award is plausible, but the boundary with Acemoglu, Robinson and Johnson (Nobel 2024) on institutions needs care.
assessment.maturity: The work spans the 1990s to the 2010s and is well established and widely taught, so the maturity is high.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity may reduce the appetite for a closely related award.
The field is broad, so the specific citation and the choice of three names are open to contest.
A Committee member in a neighbouring field has limited ability to assess the empirical identification of the cross-country evidence.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work reshaped understanding of how technology and trade shocks affect labour demand, wage inequality and regional labour markets. The task-based approach and the China-shock evidence changed both academic research and policy debate. The empirical designs are widely emulated.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the tasks framework and the trade-shock work. Hanson and Dorn are key to the China-shock evidence. Katz is central to the earlier skill-premium and technology-race literature. Selecting three of four credited names involves a judgement that could be contested, and Dorn would be a defensible alternative.
assessment.maturity: The tasks work dates from about 2003 and the trade-shock work from about 2013, so there has been time for replication, critique and extension. This is moderately mature, but some strands are still being debated.
uncertainties: Replications and critiques of the China-shock magnitudes and the long-run labour-market effects are ongoing.
Katz also appears in B014, and the Committee may prefer to recognise him elsewhere.
Related earlier work by others, such as Acemoglu, Goldin and Murphy, complicates the credit allocation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work established that reciprocity, fairness and inequity aversion explain behaviour in strategic settings, and it supplied tractable models that reconcile experiments with theory. It affects contract theory, public goods, labour markets and institutional design, and it shows how incentives can interact with social preferences.
assessment.attribution: The Fehr–Schmidt (1999) inequity-aversion model and the Fehr and Gächter experimental evidence anchor the credit. Falk is a strong contributor to the later empirical and field work, but the originating theory and the experimental programme point to Fehr and Schmidt. Bolton and Ockenfels (2000) developed a parallel model, which complicates attribution.
assessment.maturity: The core work is from 1999 to 2004, and two decades of replication and extension have followed. Behavioural economics has already been recognised (Kahneman, Thaler), so the field is well legitimised.
uncertainties: The external validity and stability of social-preference estimates are debated.
The Bolton–Ockenfels parallel work and other behavioural laureates may dilute the case.
The Committee may regard behavioural economics as already adequately recognised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model is a cornerstone of non-cooperative game theory. It gives a sharp account of how patience and outside options determine bargaining outcomes. It underpins the strategic foundations of Walrasian and decentralised-market models, as well as labour, trade and political bargaining models. The conceptual contribution is large and has lasted.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the originator and the primary name, and Rubinstein–Wolinsky (1985) extended the framework to decentralised markets. Binmore contributed to the market interpretation and the link to Nash bargaining, and Ståhl's earlier finite-horizon work is a precursor. Credit is therefore somewhat diffuse, though Rubinstein is clearly central.
assessment.maturity: The work is four decades old and fully absorbed into the canon, so the maturity is extremely high.
uncertainties: Game theory has been recognised several times (Nash, Harsanyi, Selten, Aumann, Schelling, Myerson, Maskin, Milgrom and Wilson), so the Committee may weigh the field's prior recognition.
The narrower impact on applied economics compared with the leading candidates is a concern.
Whether to include Wolinsky or to give the prize to Rubinstein alone is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work uses population-scale administrative data to document intergenerational mobility and its geographic variation. It also links neighbourhood exposure to adult outcomes, and it pioneered a new data-driven empirical approach in public economics. The policy and methodological influence is large.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader of the research programme, and Hendren is a central contributor to the causal neighbourhood-effects work. Friedman and Katz are important collaborators, so credit is shared across a large team and a three-person limit forces exclusions.
assessment.maturity: Most of the key results are from 2014 onward. Replication, robustness checks and long-run follow-up are still under way, so maturity is moderate and the work is likely to look stronger in coming years.
uncertainties: The causal interpretation of neighbourhood effects and the long-run durability of the findings remain under evaluation.
The work is more descriptive and empirical than conceptual, which may weigh against it.
Chetty also features in B042, so the field may be recognised through a different citation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification changed how economists think about credible inference. It establishes what can be learned from data under weak assumptions, and it reports bounds rather than point estimates that rely on strong assumptions. It has influenced econometric theory and policy analysis, including the treatment of selection, missing data and treatment-effect bounds.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the clear originator, with a long programme from the late 1980s. Tamer is a leading figure in the modern moment-inequality and set-identification literature, and Molinari has contributed the inference and survey of the field. The core credit to Manski is clean, and the extension to Tamer is plausible.
assessment.maturity: The foundations are over three decades old and well established. The modern inference methods are more recent and still developing.
uncertainties: The practical uptake in applied work is more limited than the conceptual influence.
Econometrics has been recognised in recent years (Heckman and McFadden, Angrist and Imbens), so the Committee must consider timing.
The line between the foundational and the more recent inference contributions is not sharp.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design supply a general framework for how a sender optimally structures information to influence decisions. The framework is tractable and has influenced theory, regulation, auctions, disclosure and platform design. It extends the information-economics tradition recognised earlier (Akerlof, Spence, Stiglitz and Vickrey).
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) are the originators, and Gentzkow is also well known for empirical media economics. Bergemann and Morris developed the closely related information-design and robust-predictions programme, and Morris has earlier foundational work on global games. The credit is shared across two overlapping lines, and a three-name limit forces a choice.
assessment.maturity: The core paper is from 2011, so this is relatively young. Applications are growing, but long-run empirical impact is limited and the framework is still developing.
uncertainties: The relative weights of Kamenica–Gentzkow and Bergemann–Morris are contestable.
The framework may be better understood in another decade.
Limited direct empirical validation compared with the other top candidates.
